chunks.section: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
chunks.text: Ke Zhang kzhan153@ucr.edu Affiliation: University of California, Riverside Sahchit Chundur smchundu@uci.edu Affiliation: University of California, Irvine Jerry Peprah Owusu jerrypeo@uci.edu Affiliation: University of California, Irvine Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi mjaq@uci.edu Affiliation: University of California, Irvine Maziar Raissi maziarr@ucr.edu Affiliation: University of California, Riverside

Many LLM agent harnesses do not put a long tool output into the model’s context window. They save it to a file, and the agent opens the file when it needs to. Earlier studies show that this form of context management can lower accuracy, but they do not explain why. We study the question with PHREEQC, a deterministic geochemistry simulator, on 158 multiple-choice questions. We find one reason: the agent stops reading the simulator’s report and answers from a file that it created itself. Both files contain the same result, but the agent’s own file shows it with more digits. When the report is delivered as a file, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4 skip it 42–60% of the time; Claude Sonnet 4.6 rarely does. We call this evidence substitution . When these agents copy the longer number into their answer, they often cut off digits instead of rounding, and so choose a wrong option. Because the simulator is deterministic, we can re-run every input file that the agents wrote (11,007 simulator calls) and locate the failure in each trajectory without a human or LLM judge. The agents compute the correct value about as often as before, but they answer with it less often. When we fix the simulation and change only how the report is delivered, GPT-5.2 loses 9.4 points of accuracy. The fix is simple: tell the agent which file to trust. The agents then read the report again, and when they see the correct value they answer correctly 99% of the time. Telling them to round correctly does not help. For anyone who builds agents that save tool output to files, this suggests a simple check: look at which file the agent actually reads before it answers, because the final accuracy alone does not show it.

LLM agents increasingly call tools whose outputs are long, such as logs, search results, and simulator reports. A harness must choose how such output reaches the model: paste it into the context, truncated to a fixed budget ( inline ), or save it to a file that the agent reads through an outline, a search tool, or ranged reads ( retrieval ). Production harnesses now write long tool results to files and return a pointer or a short preview, and report the tokens that this saves ( Rajasekaran et al., 2025 ; Katz, 2026 ; Curme & Daugherty, 2026 ) . The effect on accuracy is less clear. Controlled comparisons find that file-based delivery lowers accuracy for some models and harnesses and not for others ( Sen et al., 2026 ; McMillan, 2026 ) , and on the items used here, Zhang et al. (2026b) report that a table-of-contents interface lowers the accuracy of GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 but not of GPT-5.4 or the Claude models. These studies report final accuracy and offer explanations that they do not test, such as an added step of locating and integrating the file or a limited ability to navigate structured output. What remains unknown is where the loss arises: a wrong answer rarely shows whether the agent computed the wrong value, never saw the right one, or saw it and still answered wrongly.

A deterministic simulator makes this observable. We study LLM agents operating PHREEQC, an aqueous-geochemistry simulator ( Parkhurst & Appelo, 2013 ) whose section-structured reports reach 846.8k characters, on 158 multiple-choice items whose answer keys we re-verified by execution (Section 2.1 ). We change only how the simulator’s report reaches the agent. Our main comparison has two conditions: the report is pasted into the tool result (inline), or the agent receives a table of contents (TOC) of the report’s sections and reads the lines it wants. Section 2.2 lists all six conditions, which add keyword search and three variants of the TOC condition. Each simulation writes its result to a report. If the agent asks for it, the simulation also writes the same result to a second file, with more digits. We call the value of the correct option the keyed value ; both files contain it. Under TOC, the GPT models answer from the second file and not from the report (Figure 1 ). Because the simulator is deterministic, we can re-run every input an agent wrote. We also search every tool result that the agent received. This gives each trajectory on a numeric item three labels, with no human or model judge: did the agent compute the keyed value ( build ), did it see that value ( exposure ), and did it answer with it ( closure )? Each stage needs a different fix. A build loss needs better simulation inputs. An exposure or closure loss needs a change in what the agent reads. We therefore first locate the loss and then test the location by intervening on that stage. Our contributions are as follows.

1. Evidence substitution. Under TOC, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4 leave the simulator’s report unopened in 42–60% of trajectories and answer from their own SELECTED_OUTPUT files, which hold the same value with more digits. When that value falls between two options, they often choose the truncated one. The loss was earlier attributed to an inability to navigate the report ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) ; we find that the report is often not opened (Section 4 ). 2. An audit that locates the loss without a judge. We re-run all 11,007 simulator calls that the agents made. For each trajectory on a numeric item, this shows what the agent computed, what it saw, and what it answered. The result is simple: the agents compute the correct value about as often with TOC as with inline output, but they answer with it less often. When we continue the same simulation under both conditions, TOC still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 pp (Sections 2.3 and 4 ). 3. An intervention that tests the location. An instruction that names the report as authoritative removes report skipping and restores closure to 99% without changing build, and GPT-5.2 returns to its inline accuracy. Inlining reports that fit has the same effect; an instruction that only asks for correct rounding has none (Section 5 ).

We use PHREEQC because three of its properties let us observe each step of a tool call. First, it is deterministic: re-running an input file that an agent wrote reproduces exactly what the agent’s simulation printed. Second, its report is long and divided into sections, so retrieval is a natural way to deliver it. Third, an agent can ask it to write chosen quantities to a second file, so the same value can exist in two files in two different forms.

We use the four-option multiple-choice items of Zhang et al. (2026b) , written by one domain expert. Each describes a PHREEQC simulation setup and asks for one quantity from its output (a pH at a reaction step, a saturation index, a molality in a transport cell); several items share a setup. Reference answers come from PHREEQC 3.8.6 with a fixed, author-supplied phreeqc.dat . For numeric items, distractors typically differ from the key in the last printed digit, so they can be answered only by computing the value, not by estimating it; the remaining items ask for a comparison, a name, or a count.

We re-ran all 200 items of the original pool in PHREEQC and keep the 158 items whose printed value matches the keyed option exactly and uniquely. All results in the main text use these 158 items. Appendix A gives the procedure and shows that the full pool leads to the same conclusions. As a reference point, a PHREEQC user with eight years of experience who did not write the items, working with the simulator, answered 60 of 75 sampled verified items correctly and abstained on 13 whose simulation matched no option (Appendix H ).

Each agent has four tools — write_file , read_file (optionally with a line range), list_file , and execute_phreeqc — and works in an isolated workspace for at most 24 steps, committing to an answer by writing it to a file. PHREEQC writes a formatted report ( result.out ) that prints each quantity at the precision the answer options use; agents may also add SELECTED_OUTPUT or USER_PUNCH blocks, which write chosen quantities to separate files with more digits. The conditions differ in what execute_phreeqc returns and in the system-prompt line that describes it (Table 1 ; Appendix B ). We refer to the first as inline and to TOC and Grep as retrieval . The simulation, the tools, and the step budget are the same in all of them.

We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash Preview through their APIs: the Claude models at temperature 0 without extended thinking, the GPT and Gemini models at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting. Without the simulator, no model exceeds 46.2% with direct or chain-of-thought prompting (the majority-label rate is 32.9%), so the items require the tool (Appendix B , Table 8 ). Gemini 3 Flash gives no parseable answer on 46% of items even inline, so we report it in Appendix G and leave it out of the analyses below.

Each model has one headline inline run and one headline TOC run. We rerun TOC three times for Sonnet and the GPT models and inline once for the GPT models, and run Grep and the interventions on a subset of models (Table 7 ). Rates are averaged over runs; counts use each trajectory once. Our primary comparison is TOC against inline per model, with every run pooled per item, 95% item-bootstrap intervals, and sign-flip permutation tests Holm-corrected over the five models.

For every agent run we store the full trace: the model’s messages, every tool call, and every tool result. We analyze these logs offline. For every full-agent trajectory with a complete log (5,773) we rebuilt each input file as it was when the agent executed it and re-ran it with the same binary and database: 11,007 simulator calls in all. As a check, we compared the re-run of the last execution with the stored report in 5,009 numeric trajectories. The two are identical in 4,971; the rest differ only in line order. For the 137 items with numeric answers we then ask three questions (Figure 1 ), matching values at the precision the options are printed with: • Build ( p p ): did the agent compute the keyed value, that is, did any of its own simulations print it? • Exposure ( s s ): given that it was computed, did the agent see the value, inline or through a read or search result? • Closure ( c c ): given that the agent saw the value, did it answer with it, that is, choose the keyed option? Accuracy equals p ​ s ​ c p\,s\,c plus the share of answers that were correct without the keyed value in view. We call these answers unsupported ; they are nearest-option picks and guesses. Appendix D attributes each condition’s accuracy change to these four terms. We also record the file from which each seen value came. Matching is numeric, so a number can also match on a line that prints another quantity. Two checks address this. Automatic and manual stage labels agree on 52 of 58 numeric trajectories that we read by hand. And the results hold on the 93 numeric items whose keyed value occurs only once in the reference report (Appendix C ).

chunks.section: GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose accuracy under TOC.
chunks.text: Pooling every run per item, TOC changes accuracy relative to inline output by − - 11.3 pp for GPT-5.1 and − - 7.9 pp for GPT-5.2 (Figure 2 ). Zhang et al. (2026b) reported the same net effect. We reproduce it on verified items and with reruns. The GPT-5.1 difference is significant after Holm correction over the five models. The GPT-5.2 difference is not, but with the simulation held fixed the change is − - 9.4 pp, with an interval that excludes zero (Section 4 ). One keyword-search run, which uses no PHREEQC section structure, shows a similar cost (Table 2 ).

chunks.section: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.4 show no detectable net cost.
chunks.text: Their pooled differences are within 1 pp of zero, with intervals that include zero (Figure 2 ).

chunks.section: 4 Agents Answer from Their Own Output
Under retrieval, agents substitute their own output for the report.
chunks.text: Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them. In most trajectories they read their own selected-output files (Table 2 , Skip and Own; Figure 1 a). They define such files about as often inline (Table 12 , Def.), but there the report is already in context and they answer from it. We call this evidence substitution : leaving the tool’s canonical report unopened and answering from output that the agent defined itself. Sonnet skips the report in about one of ten TOC trajectories. Figure 3 shows one trajectory of this kind in full: the agent defines a selected-output file in its first input, reads that file after the run, and answers with the truncation of the value it prints, although the index it received points to the section of the report that prints the keyed value. chunks.text: Figure 3: A GPT-5.1 TOC trajectory on item 121 (pH after the first reaction step; options A 2.750, B 2.751, C 2.748, D 2.745; key B), with tool results abridged and “/” marking line breaks. The agent answers A, the truncation of the 2.75065 in its own selected-output file, and never reads the report, which prints the keyed 2.751.

chunks.section: Answering from one’s own output fails in two ways.
chunks.text: Closure. The report prints each quantity at the precision the options use, whereas selected-output files print more digits, so an agent reading them must round, and the GPT models often truncate instead. A typical case reads “gives pH = 2.75065, which rounds to 2.750” for a keyed value of 2.751. We call a trajectory a trap case when the value the agent saw rounds to the keyed value but truncates to another option. In trap cases under TOC, GPT-5.2 chose the truncated option 26/35 times, GPT-5.1 19/27, and Sonnet 1/35 (Table 2 , Trap). For the GPT models the truncated value always came from the agent’s own file, never from the report. They chose the truncated option more often when it is a literal prefix of the printed number (72%) than when the two are printed in different notations (39%). This suggests digit matching, not rounding (Appendix D ). Counting every truncated answer as correct removes most of the TOC-minus-inline difference of GPT-5.2 and about a fifth of GPT-5.1’s (Table 15 ). Section 5 tests whether this is only a rounding error. Exposure. The remaining loss arises one step earlier. Sometimes the agent computed the keyed value but never saw it. In most of these cases it had skipped the report, and its own file printed a different quantity, such as a log activity, from which it answered (Appendix D ).

chunks.section: What the agents compute does not change.
chunks.text: The audit shows that the loss is not in computation. Within each of GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1, the share of trajectories that compute the keyed value is similar under every delivery, while exposure and closure fall under TOC and Grep (Table 2 , Build, Exposure, and Closure). Attributing the accuracy change to the stages gives the same picture, with closure the largest term for GPT-5.2 (Appendix D , Figure 7 ).

chunks.section: The loss persists with the simulation held fixed.
chunks.text: To separate delivery from computation, we take GPT-5.2’s logged inline run and stop it at its first successful simulation, on 131 numeric items. From that point we continue the same history twice: once with the report inline, and once with the TOC (Appendix E ). Both arms share the files, system prompt, reading tools, and remaining turns; they can read files and submit an answer but not rerun the simulator. Over three paired repeats, TOC changes accuracy by − - 9.4 pp [ − - 14.5, − - 4.6] (Table 3 ). The loss is as large on the reports that fit inline and on the items whose frozen report contains the keyed value (Appendix E ). Table 3: GPT-5.2 replay on 131 frozen checkpoints. chunks.section: GPT-5.4 makes the same choice without answer options.
chunks.text: Evidence substitution could be a reaction to options that differ only in the last digit. In a fill-in-the-blank version of the items, which asks for the numeric value itself, GPT-5.4 under TOC receives no part of the report on 97 of 145 items and reads a file of its own in every such trajectory; 87 of 97 of these answers carry more digits than the report prints (Appendix F ).

chunks.section: GPT-5.4 shows the same behavior without a net loss.
chunks.text: GPT-5.4 substitutes evidence as well: it skips the report in about four of ten TOC trajectories and chooses the truncated option in about half of the trap cases (Table 2 , Trap). Its net change is nevertheless indistinguishable from zero, while its simulations compute the keyed value more often under TOC (Table 2 , Build; Appendix D ). A reading of this model’s TOC errors by the benchmark’s item author, made before our audit existed, names the same failure: in 12 of 55 errors the right value was present in the agent’s output and not used (Appendix H ).

Figure 4: Report skipping and closure under each condition. An instruction to round correctly (TOC+Round) does not reduce skipping and does not raise closure; naming the report (TOC+Report) or inlining reports that fit (Hybrid), the two bracketed conditions, removes the skipping and restores closure. TOC is the control run made alongside the interventions (GPT-5.4: its TOC reruns). TOC+Round and Hybrid were run for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, so GPT-5.4’s line joins TOC and TOC+Report directly. If the loss arises because agents answer from their own higher-precision files, changing which output they answer from should remove it without changing what they compute. We compare three variants with a fresh TOC run (TOC control): TOC+Report, Hybrid, and TOC+Round (Figure 4 and Table 2 ). TOC+Report adds the following to the TOC tool description and to every tool result: “IMPORTANT: The authoritative values are in result.out, printed at the precision the answer options use. Before answering, read the section of result.out that contains the quantity you need and take the value exactly as printed there. Do not answer from SELECTED_OUTPUT or USER_PUNCH files: they print unrounded values that can match a neighboring option.” Hybrid adds no instruction and inlines reports that fit within 100,000 characters.

chunks.section: The report instruction changes what agents read and removes the closure loss.
chunks.text: With the report instruction, report skipping falls below 2%, the agents rarely read their own output files, and no trajectory falls into the truncation trap (Figure 4 , Table 2 ). Closure rises to about 99%, while build stays within run-to-run variation. GPT-5.2 returns to its inline accuracy. GPT-5.1 gains about eight points over the TOC control but stays about five points below its inline accuracy. That gap is not in closure (Appendix D ).

chunks.section: Is the loss only a rounding error?
chunks.text: The example in Figure 1 invites a simpler explanation: the agents may just be bad at rounding. The two explanations predict different things. If the problem is rounding, an instruction to round correctly should help. If the problem is which file the agent reads, naming the report should help, and a rounding instruction should not. To test this, TOC+Round replaces the instruction with one that gives the rounding rule and names no file: “IMPORTANT: The answer options give each value at a fixed precision. If a value you read has more digits than the options, round it to the options’ precision to the nearest value; do not truncate digits. Choose the option that equals the correctly rounded value.” The rounding instruction does not help. Agents still skip the report about as often as under TOC, closure is about 82%, no higher than under the TOC control, and they still choose the truncated option in about seven of ten trap cases, although told not to truncate (Table 4 ). Accuracy changes by − - 3.8 (GPT-5.2) and + + 2.8 pp (GPT-5.1) against the TOC control, with no consistent gain. The same agents answer correctly when the report is in front of them and they answer from it: with inline output, closure is 94–99% (Table 2 ). Truncation is also not the whole loss: with every truncated answer counted as correct, GPT-5.1 still changes by − - 8.5 pp (Table 15 ). The loss is therefore not a rounding error on its own. The agents truncate because they answer from a file that prints more digits, and they stop when they are directed to the value that is already printed at the right precision.

chunks.section: The report instruction also lifts GPT-5.4.
chunks.text: With the report instruction, GPT-5.4 reaches 81.6% in both runs, about eight points above both its TOC runs and its inline runs, with intervals that exclude zero. Report skipping falls to zero and closure returns to 99%, while the build gain of retrieval remains, so the instruction removes the loss from evidence substitution while keeping what retrieval adds.

chunks.section: Inlining what fits has the same effect.
chunks.text: Over three runs of Hybrid, report skipping nearly disappears and closure returns to about its inline level (Table 2 ). Accuracy rises over the TOC control by + + 4.6 (GPT-5.2) and + + 8.0 pp (GPT-5.1). Relative to the inline runs, GPT-5.2 is within about 1 pp and GPT-5.1 is again about five points lower, with the residual outside closure.

Both interventions restore closure without changing build, and for GPT-5.2 the paired replay shows the loss with computation fixed. So the closure loss comes from which file the agent answers from. Hybrid needs no knowledge of the tool; the instruction keeps retrieval but must name the canonical output.

chunks.section: Retrieval adds a choice of evidence.
chunks.text: The two deliveries make the same report obtainable: every number in the inline report is one read away, and for GPT-5.2, with the simulation held fixed, the loss remains on reports that fit inline. What differs is which output the agent answers from. In our setting, retrieval turns reading the report into a choice of evidence. Inline, one source is in view; under retrieval, the report competes with the files the agent wrote itself, and models that choose badly lose accuracy. The instruction works because it makes that choice for them.

The substitution costs accuracy here because the two outputs print the same value differently and the items require the report’s precision. This is the condition under which the mechanism applies: a tool with a canonical output, and an agent that can define an output of its own whose form need not match the form in which answers are checked.

In our setting, final accuracy does not show where the loss arises, and for GPT-5.4 it does not show the substitution at all. Stating which output is authoritative removed the substitution; inlining outputs that fit had the same effect and needs no knowledge of the tool.

The agent–computer interface, including how files are viewed and searched, changes what software-engineering agents achieve ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Long tool responses in context degrade function calling ( Kate et al., 2025 ) , and harnesses respond by truncating, masking, or compressing observations ( Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) or by writing them to files that the agent opens or searches ( Abramovich et al., 2025 ; Rajasekaran et al., 2025 ; Katz, 2026 ; Curme & Daugherty, 2026 ) . File-based delivery helps when the material is far larger than the context window ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . For material that fits, controlled comparisons report effects of both signs: Sen et al. (2026) find that delivering search results as files lowers accuracy in nine of ten harness–model pairs, and state that they lack trace-level attribution; McMillan (2026) finds that delivering a database schema as files slightly helps frontier models and hurts open-weight models. On the items we use, Zhang et al. (2026b) report that a table-of-contents interface lowers the accuracy of GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 and attribute this to navigation ability. We reproduce that net effect on verified items and revise the explanation: we locate the loss within individual trajectories and test the location by intervention.

chunks.section: Whether agents use the evidence available to them.
chunks.text: Models do not always use context that contains what they need ( Joren et al., 2025 ) , and agents often see relevant content without acting on it ( Engländer et al., 2026 ) . Closest to the behavior we report, Roh & Han (2026) show from tool-call logs that agentic-RAG controllers often answer without reading the passages they retrieved, and that an environment rule that rejects such answers raises accuracy. Agents also rarely request the rest of an over-long tool response ( Petrova et al., 2026 ) or recall observations that were moved to external storage ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . In these studies an agent that skips the evidence has no other source of the answer. In ours it has one: a second output of the same tool call, which holds the correct value in another representation. Studies of source preference find that models favor generated or self-authored text over retrieved text when the two disagree ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Druck & Smith, 2026 ) ; our two outputs agree in value, and the cost arises when the value is transcribed. Rounding to significant digits is unreliable in isolation ( Yang et al., 2025 ) ; we observe truncation in place of rounding when a value is copied from a source with more digits.

Agent failures are usually attributed to a step or an agent: by human or model judges ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , by an attributor trained on counterfactual replays ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , or by replaying the agent with a proposed repair ( Lin et al., 2026 ) . Other diagnostics separate evidence that was never obtained from evidence that was obtained and not used: RAGChecker with model-based claim checking ( Ru et al., 2024 ) , Liu et al. (2026) with human relevance labels for search agents, and Xie et al. (2026) with rule-scored hits for messages between agents. Xie et al. (2026) decompose communication loss into externalization, absorption, and action closure; our exposure stage is closest to their externalization, and our closure stage merges their absorption and action closure, which we do not separate. Deterministic scoring of recorded tool traces ( Flynt, 2026 ) and replay from a frozen state ( Pakhomov & Nijkamp, 2026 ) have also been proposed. A deterministic simulator adds a label for the stage that precedes these: re-executing the inputs the agent itself wrote shows whether it computed the target value at all. Agents for scientific software are usually studied on one package and graded on outcomes: OpenFOAM cases that run ( Yue et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , COMSOL targets ( Mudur et al., 2025 ) , or molecular-dynamics subtasks ( Campbell et al., 2025 ) ; SUPER checks whether expected outputs appear in executed cells ( Bogin et al., 2024 ) .

All models are closed and accessed through their APIs. Evidence substitution appears in all three GPT models and rarely in Claude Sonnet 4.6, the Claude model with full trajectory logs; we do not determine which model property drives this difference.

The Claude agents ran at temperature 0 without extended thinking, and the GPT agents at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting, so we do not know whether the effect persists with explicit reasoning. We test one wording of each instruction.

On 158 PHREEQC items, three GPT models that receive the simulator’s report through retrieval often leave it unopened, answer from an output file of their own design, and truncate its value. Re-executing every logged trajectory shows that they compute the keyed value about as often as before; for GPT-5.2, holding the simulation fixed confirms that the loss comes from the delivery. Naming the authoritative output, or inlining reports that fit, removes the substitution; asking for correct rounding does not. Re-executing the agents’ own inputs in a deterministic tool showed where the answers were lost, which final accuracy did not.

Every item in the 200-item pool was re-executed in PHREEQC 3.8.6 with the frozen phreeqc.dat . The inline description discourages additional reads, and the retrieval descriptions require them; part of the difference in reading behavior between inline and retrieval conditions may therefore be induced by the descriptions rather than by the return value alone; the paired replay, whose arms share one system prompt, still shows the loss (Appendix E ). The TOC+Report instruction both names the authoritative file and gives a reason to prefer it; TOC+Round gives only the rounding rule and names no file.

Every execute_phreeqc call returns the exit status, the last 4,000 characters of PHREEQC’s standard output and error, and the names and sizes of the files the run created. Inline adds the report, cut to its first and last 50,000 characters with a truncation marker when it is longer than 100,000. TOC adds an index of the report’s dash-delimited section headers with their starting lines, at most 50 entries (the first and last 25 when a report has more), and the hint “Use read_file with start_line/end_line to read specific sections.” In the headline TOC runs and the TOC reruns the index was empty for reports longer than 100,000 characters, so on those items all four TOC runs use one separate run with the index built; all other runs build it for every report. Hybrid adds the report when it fits and otherwise the index and the report length; Grep adds only the report’s line count. TOC+Report and TOC+Round return the TOC payload with their instruction appended to the hint, so the agent sees the instruction in the system prompt and again in every execute_phreeqc result. With a line range, read_file returns the requested lines; without one it returns a file of up to 20,000 characters whole and otherwise its first and last 80 lines (no content in Grep). For every execute_phreeqc call we rebuilt the input from the agent’s preceding write_file events and re-ran it with the same PHREEQC 3.8.6 binary and database (11,007 calls, 10,605 distinct inputs). The produced corpus is every output of these executions; the seen corpus is every tool result the agent received that carries simulator output (inline payloads, read_file results on the report or selected-output files, and search matches). A keyed value counts as present if a printed number equals the option at its precision, or rounds to it when printed with more digits; numbers on a rounding midpoint match both neighbors; for quantities described as dissolved, precipitated, or changed, the sign is ignored; specific-conductance options match only on conductance lines; the echo of the input in the report is excluded. A trajectory is labeled build if the keyed value was never produced, exposure if it was produced but never seen, and closure if it was seen but the answer was wrong; trajectories without a gradable answer and wrong answers on non-numeric items are counted separately. Because matching is numeric, a printed number could also match the keyed value on a line that reports a different quantity. On the 93 numeric items whose keyed value occurs only once in the reference report, where this is least likely, the TOC terms are closure − - 9.8 [ − - 15.4, − - 4.5] and exposure − - 3.2 [ − - 6.5, − - 0.0] for GPT-5.2, closure − - 6.8 [ − - 11.2, − - 2.9] and exposure − - 4.9 [ − - 8.0, − - 2.5] for GPT-5.1, and closure − - 7.4 [ − - 11.7, − - 3.8] and exposure − - 3.3 [ − - 6.3, − - 0.2] for GPT-5.4 (pp, 95% item-bootstrap intervals). Among correct numeric answers of the Claude and GPT agents, the keyed value was seen in 69–95% of trajectories; the remainder are mostly nearest-option picks when no option value was produced, which we report as unsupported answers. Re-execution moved only 8 trajectories from build to exposure. Of the 1,039 build failures of the Claude and GPT agents, 926 produced none of the four option values, and re-running the agents’ inputs with PHREEQC’s full default printing recovered the keyed value in 5.

Independently of the automatic labels, we read 68 trajectories: 12 TOC losses each for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 and 6 Grep losses for GPT-5.2 (items wrong under retrieval but correct inline, each read together with its inline trajectory, 60 in all), and 8 Sonnet TOC failures. Seven of the 24 TOC losses were caused by the retrieval channel (the inline run had the value in context, while the TOC run never saw it or misread its own selected output), two were mistakes with the value in hand, and fifteen were build failures, seven of which the inline run also had and answered correctly by choosing the nearest option. Losses selected on the outcome are therefore dominated by build failures that churn between runs and net out, which is why we rely on the decomposition rather than on item-level losses. On the 58 numeric trajectories in this sample, the automatic stage (build, exposure, closure, or correct with the keyed value in view) agrees with the manual one in 52 cases. Five of the six disagreements count a matching number printed for another reaction step or solution as the keyed value, which moves a build failure into exposure or closure (or, once, a lucky answer into a supported one); the sixth misses a value the agent saw only as a logarithm. The sample was selected on outcomes, so this agreement rate is indicative rather than a population estimate. Navigating to the wrong report section occurred once. All eight Sonnet failures were build failures. Representative excerpts: “gives pH = 2.75065, which rounds to 2.750” (key 2.751); “Talc: 23.333 mol … The mineral that dissolved the most is Talc” (final amount read as amount reacted; the inline run with the same input saw the change column).

Pooling every run per item, TOC changes accuracy relative to inline output by − - 11.3 pp [ − - 18.0, − - 4.9] for GPT-5.1 and − - 7.9 pp [ − - 14.9, − - 0.9] for GPT-5.2 (Figure 2 and Table 8 ; the pool includes the TOC control run of Section 5 ). After Holm correction over the five models, the GPT-5.1 difference is significant ( p = 0.005 p=0.005 ) and the GPT-5.2 difference is not ( p = 0.128 p=0.128 ; unadjusted 0.032 0.032 ); with the simulation held fixed, GPT-5.2’s TOC cost is − - 9.4 pp [ − - 14.5, − - 4.6] (Section 4 ). Resampling the 19 setups instead of items gives intervals of [ − - 19.1, − - 2.9] (GPT-5.1) and [ − - 16.2, + + 1.0] (GPT-5.2), and leaving out any one setup moves the estimates only within − - 14.0 to − - 9.7 and − - 10.9 to − - 5.8 pp. For both models, the two inline runs score higher than every TOC run and the Grep run (Table 9 ). The Grep run, which uses no PHREEQC section structure, shows a similar cost. The pooled differences of Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.4 are − - 0.6, − - 0.5, and + + 0.2 pp, with intervals that include zero; for GPT-5.4 the stage terms below have opposite signs. Figure 7: Where the accuracy change under TOC comes from, relative to each model’s logged inline run on the 137 numeric items (Shapley attribution, pp; stage rates and 95% intervals in Tables 10 and 11 ). Exposure and closure are negative in all three models; in GPT-5.4 a gain in build offsets part of them.

For GPT-5.2 under TOC, closure accounts for − - 7.7 of the − - 11.4 pp change on numeric items, with an interval that excludes zero, and exposure for − - 2.5 pp. For GPT-5.1 the loss splits about evenly between exposure and closure, each with an interval that excludes zero (Tables 10 and 11 ). Grep shows the same pattern. These totals are relative to the single logged inline run and cover numeric items only, so they differ from the pooled contrast in Table 8 . Figure 7 shows the attribution for the three GPT models. Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in 60.3% and 53.0% of trajectories, and Sonnet in 10.5% (Table 13 ). Trap cases make up about two thirds of the TOC trajectories that saw the keyed value and still answered wrongly. Answers were nearly always correct when the keyed value was seen as the report prints it, and correct in 72.5% (GPT-5.2) and 66.3% (GPT-5.1) of the trajectories that saw it only with more digits. When the agent received both the report’s form of the keyed value and a value that truncates to another option, which happens mostly when the report is inline, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 answered correctly in 3 of 12 trajectories (inline and Hybrid runs) and Sonnet in 32 of 33 (TOC runs). When the keyed value was computed but never seen, the agent had skipped the report in 14 of 17 cases for GPT-5.1 and 6 of 7 for GPT-5.2. Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 take more steps than inline (9.1 versus 7.2 steps), and one of the 30 retrieval losses that we read by hand involved a wrong report section.

GPT-5.4’s two inline runs scored 70.9% and 76.6%; the second has trajectory logs and is the baseline of the decomposition. GPT-5.4 skips the report in 41.8% of TOC trajectories (Table 13 ). Relative to its logged inline run, TOC costs it about ten points in exposure and closure ( − - 2.6 and − - 7.2 pp), about as much as GPT-5.2, and it gains + + 4.1 [ + + 0.0, + + 8.1] pp in build (Table 10 ). On this basis (numeric items, three TOC reruns against the logged inline run) the net change is − - 4.4 [ − - 12.4, + + 3.4] pp, and pooled over all runs and items it is + + 0.2 pp. Neither is distinguishable from zero, while its exposure and closure terms are both negative with intervals that exclude zero.

With the report instruction, report skipping falls to 0.0% (GPT-5.2) and 1.6% (GPT-5.1), and 99% of the correct numeric answers that saw the keyed value took it from the report. Closure rises to 98.8% and 99.2%, and build is unchanged within run-to-run variation (Table 12 ). Accuracy rises over all five TOC runs by + + 7.9 and + + 6.3 pp ( + + 7.1 pp [ + + 1.9, + + 12.4] averaged over the two models) and over the TOC control by + + 3.5 and + + 7.9 pp, a comparison limited by one control run per model. GPT-5.1 remains below its inline accuracy ( − - 5.1 pp [ − - 11.4, + + 0.9]), with the residual in the build, exposure, and unsupported terms. Under the rounding instruction, the agents choose the truncated option in 17/25 (GPT-5.2) and 14/19 (GPT-5.1) trap cases. Accuracy changes by + + 0.6 and + + 1.2 pp relative to all TOC runs and by − - 3.8 and + + 2.8 pp relative to the TOC control. TOC+Report exceeds TOC+Round by + + 7.3 pp [ + + 0.6, + + 13.9] and + + 5.1 pp [ − - 1.6, + + 12.0]. With the report instruction, GPT-5.4 reaches 81.6% in both runs, + + 7.8 pp [ + + 2.2, + + 13.6] above its TOC runs and + + 7.9 pp [ + + 2.5, + + 13.3] above its inline runs. Report skipping falls to 0.0% and closure rises to 99.0%, and the build gain under TOC remains ( + + 3.4 pp relative to inline). Over three runs, Hybrid raises accuracy over the TOC control by + + 4.6 (GPT-5.2) and + + 8.0 pp (GPT-5.1). Relative to the inline runs, GPT-5.2 changes by + + 1.2 pp and GPT-5.1 by − - 5.0 pp, with GPT-5.1’s residual outside closure.

chunks.section: How much of the loss is truncation.
chunks.text: In all 60 TOC trajectories in which a GPT model chose the option to which a received value truncates, that value came from the agent’s own file and never from the report. The models chose the truncated option in 72% of the cases in which that option is a literal prefix of the printed value (105 of 145) and in 39% of those in which the two are printed in different notations (12 of 31); the two groups cover different items. Table 15 recomputes the TOC-minus-inline difference on the runs with trajectory logs after counting as correct every answer that chose the option to which a received value truncates. The comparison uses the three TOC reruns and the TOC control against the logged inline run of each model, so its first column differs slightly from the pooled contrast in Table 8 . For GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.4 the remaining difference is within about 3 pp of zero; for GPT-5.1 it is − - 8.5 pp with an interval that excludes zero, and lies mostly outside closure (Figure 7 ). We take the first execution returning exit code zero in GPT-5.2’s logged inline run, before its result reaches the model. Of the 137 numeric items, 131 have such a checkpoint; the remaining six have no successful execution. Selection uses the execution status, independently of the original final answer or whether the output contains the keyed value. We reconstruct the visible history and workspace by replaying the preceding file writes and PHREEQC calls in order, including earlier failed executions. For the 115 untruncated reports, re-execution matches the recorded report after normalizing path and timing lines and separator rules; the other 16 original returns contain only the capped head and tail. Both delivery arms use the same reconstructed files, verified by hashes.

Only the pending execution result differs: the inline arm returns the report with the usual 100,000-character cap, whereas TOC returns its section index, built at every report size. The arms share a common system prompt, the visible history, file-reading tools, and the remaining budget of 24 − s 24-s assistant turns, where s s is the execution’s turn. They can list or read the frozen files and submit final_answer.txt ; simulation files remain fixed. We run 3 continuations per item and condition with GPT-5.2’s API defaults and a 4,096-completion-token cap per call. Item order and the order of the two arms within each pair are shuffled with a fixed seed (20261011), and the paired arms run consecutively. The first repeat was inspected before the two additional repeats were run. These 786 continuations are counted separately from the full-agent trajectories in Appendix C .

Table 3 in the main text gives the counts per repeat. For each item we average the three paired accuracy differences, then average across the 131 items. A missing submitted answer counts as incorrect; one TOC continuation in repeat 2 exhausts its remaining turns. We compute a percentile 95% interval with 50,000 paired-item bootstrap resamples (seed 20261011), retaining all three repeats of each sampled item. The mean difference is − - 9.4 pp, with interval [ − - 14.5, − - 4.6]. As a sensitivity check for shared setups, we resample the 19 setups with all their items and repeats, retaining the item-weighted mean; the interval is [ − - 13.9, − - 5.2].

The 115 frozen reports that fit inline yield 75.4% inline and 65.2% under TOC ( − - 10.1 pp). For the 16 longer reports the corresponding accuracies are 41.7% and 37.5%. Using the matching rule in Appendix C , the keyed value is present in the frozen report for 84 items; accuracy on these items is 93.7% inline and 83.7% under TOC. The fixed outputs therefore retain the same value while the delivery choice changes how often the agent answers correctly.

chunks.section: Appendix F Evidence Use without Answer Options
chunks.text: The fill-in-the-blank version of the items keeps each question stem, removes the four options, and asks for the numeric value, which is graded against the key with a per-item absolute tolerance (for most items just under half a unit of the key’s last printed digit). It covers the 182 items of the pool whose answer is a number without a unit; 145 of them are verified items. The agent, its tools, and the TOC interface are those of Section 2.2 ; the system prompt differs in the lines that state the task and the answer format. We analyze the one logged run, GPT-5.4 under TOC, which answers 59.3% of the 145 items within tolerance, against 1.4% and 2.8% for Direct and CoT prompting. Table 16 splits the trajectories by whether any part of result.out reached the agent. The agent skips the report on 97 items (66.9%), and each time it reads a file that its own simulation wrote. 87 of 97 of these answers carry more significant digits than the key, which has the precision of the report, so the printed answer itself shows that it was not taken from the report. Because the grader accepts a value within tolerance, answering from the more precise file is not penalized here as it is with options one digit apart, and the two groups differ little in accuracy. The run shows that the choice of evidence does not depend on the options; it does not measure a cost of retrieval, since no inline fill-in-the-blank run with logs is available for comparison. A PHREEQC user with eight years of experience who did not write the items and took no part in running or analyzing the agents, answered a worksheet of 75 verified items: five from each of 15 setups, chosen by a seeded hash that uses neither answer letters nor model outcomes. The other setups were left out because their text does not fully determine the reference input (Appendix A ) or because they have too few verified items. The participant worked offline with PHREEQC 3.8.6 and the frozen database, saw no answer keys and no model output, received no feedback, and could choose “E” when no option matched the simulation or the answer was unknown. The session took about four and a half hours. The participant answered 60 of the 75 items correctly (80.0%), chose a wrong option on 2, and chose E on 13 (Table 18 ). For each of the 13 the participant recorded the value obtained or the information found missing, so each followed a simulation that matched no option, a build failure in the terms of Section 2.3 . Of the 62 answers committed to an option, 60 were correct. The agents have no such option and must commit to one of four.
